youtube.baslik: Single-Sided Deafness and the Cochlear Implant Option | Lesson 246 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
What options are there for someone with one normal ear and one deaf ear? In this lesson we cover the everyday effects of single-sided deafness, how CROS and bone-conduction devices compare with a cochlear implant, outcomes for localization and hearing in noise, the effect on tinnitus, and key points in candidacy.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Van de Heyning et al. (2008), Incapacitating unilateral tinnitus in single-sided deafness treated by cochlear implantation, Annals of Otology, Rhinology and Laryngology; Arndt et al. (2011), Comparison of pseudobinaural hearing to real binaural hearing rehabilitation after cochlear implantation in patients with unilateral deafness and tinnitus, Otology and Neurotology; Wolfe, Cochlear Implants; Katz, Handbook of Clinical Audiology.

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.alt: CROS, bone conduction and cochlear implants
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn the options for people with one normal ear and one deaf ear, and where the cochlear implant fits.
We will compare signal rerouting, bone-conduction devices and the implant for localization, hearing in noise and tinnitus.
In this example, hearing in the right ear is within normal limits.
In the left ear, masked testing shows a profound loss; at the high frequencies there is no response at the audiometer limit.
When one ear is near normal and the other has too much loss to benefit from a hearing aid, this is called single-sided deafness.
When the better ear also has a mild to moderate loss and the ears differ clearly, this is called asymmetric hearing loss.
These people hear the person in front of them easily in quiet; so the problem is often underestimated.
Yet they have clear difficulties in the noisy, busy settings of everyday life.
Spatial hearing, that is, locating sounds and separating them by direction, requires two ears.
When speech comes from the deaf side, the head shadow weakens it, and less of it reaches the good ear.
If the noise comes from the good ear's side, understanding speech becomes even harder.
People describe constant effort to follow conversation in a crowd, and being tired by the end of the day.
Many people also have tinnitus in the deaf ear, which can clearly affect quality of life.
Children with a unilateral loss have a higher risk of difficulties at school and in language; they are followed closely.
Common causes of single-sided deafness in adults include sudden hearing loss, inner ear infections and Meniere's disease.
Vestibular schwannoma surgery and temporal bone fractures can also cause single-sided deafness.
In children, congenital cytomegalovirus infection is an important cause.
Some children born with single-sided deafness have a deficient cochlear nerve; so imaging comes before the implant decision.
Besides the cause, we ask how long the loss has been present, because this is one of the factors that most affects implant outcome.
When the cochlear nerve has been cut during surgery, an implant is not an option.
For some people, information and communication strategies are enough: for example, sitting with the good ear toward the speaker in meetings.
Contralateral routing of signals, or CROS, carries sound from the deaf side wirelessly to a receiver on the good ear.
Bone-conduction devices carry sound from the deaf side to the cochlea on the good side through skull vibration.
Unlike the others, a cochlear implant stimulates the deaf ear itself again.
We covered CROS and bone-conduction devices in earlier lessons; now let us compare them with the implant.
The choice among options is made after unbiased information, together with the person's goals and everyday settings.
In this drawing, sound comes from the deaf ear's side; the ear on the other side hears normally.
Because of the head shadow, speech reaches the good ear weakened, especially at high frequencies.
CROS and bone-conduction devices overcome the shadow by carrying this sound to the good ear; speech from the poor side is heard better.
But in both systems, all sounds finally reach a single cochlea; in other words, the person still hears with one ear.
So localization does not improve, and if noise comes from the poor side, the noise is carried to the good ear as well.
A cochlear implant gives the deaf ear its own input back; the brain again receives information from two separate ears.
Although the acoustic sound of the normal ear and the electric sound of the implant differ, the brain can learn over time to combine them.
CROS needs no surgery, can be tried at once and easily stopped; so it is often the first option tried.
The receiver on the good ear is usually fitted with an open tip; but some people find wearing devices on both ears bothersome.
With a bone-conduction device, vibration loses some strength crossing the skull to the other cochlea, especially at high frequencies.
This device can be tried without surgery on a band; permanent use, however, requires an implant placed in the bone.
A cochlear implant requires surgery, and results require months of regular use and listening training.
For each option, care, cost, reimbursement and any future need for magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, are also discussed.
In the end, the right option depends on the person's everyday settings and which difficulty they most want to solve.
Studies show that in single-sided deafness, an implant improves localization more than CROS and bone-conduction devices do.
Localization often does not reach the level of people with normal hearing, but it gives a noticeable improvement in daily life.
The gain for understanding in noise depends on which side the speech and the noise come from.
The gain is clearest when speech comes from the implanted side; when both come from the front, the gain is smaller.
Many people are reported to have clearly less tinnitus in the deaf ear while the implant is on.
People usually report less listening effort and a better quality of life; but the benefit varies from person to person.

cumleler.yazi: In 2008, Van de Heyning and colleagues reported that an implant reduced tinnitus in people with single-sided deafness and severe tinnitus.
cumleler.ses: In two thousand eight, Van de Heyning and colleagues reported that an implant reduced tinnitus in people with single-sided deafness and severe tinnitus.

cumleler: This schematic graph shows the general picture seen in such studies; the values are not real data.
For most people, tinnitus severity drops clearly while the implant is on.
In some people the effect partly persists when the implant is switched off; in others, tinnitus returns to its earlier level.
Tinnitus should not be expected to disappear completely; so the person is given a realistic expectation.
Tinnitus is not considered a reason for an implant on its own, but together with hearing goals.

cumleler.yazi: Some centers in Europe have implanted single-sided deafness since the 2000s; in the US, this use was approved in 2019.
cumleler.ses: Some centers in Europe have implanted single-sided deafness since the two thousands; in the US, this use was approved in twenty nineteen.

cumleler: These approvals covered people aged five years and older.
The definition of single-sided deafness required a four-frequency average of thirty decibels HL or better in the good ear.
One approval required at least one month's trial of a hearing aid, CROS or similar device without benefit before the implant.
For asymmetric loss, more loss is allowed in the better ear, and a clear difference between the two ears is required.

cumleler: In adults, the shorter the duration of deafness, the better implant outcomes usually are; so evaluation should not be delayed.
In children born with single-sided deafness, the auditory pathway of the deaf ear receives no stimulation for years.
In these children, meaningful benefit is expected only if the implant is done early; done late, results may be very limited.
Imaging should show that the cochlear nerve is intact.
Because the normal ear stays dominant, regular use and getting used to the implant take patience; motivation clearly affects outcome.
If the person's goals are unclear or their expectations unrealistic, more detailed counseling is needed before the decision.

maddeler.metin: Stream sound to the implant only

cumleler: In single-sided deafness, the normal ear hears sound much more clearly, so at first the brain may ignore the implant.
To train the implanted ear alone, a sound source such as a phone or an audiobook can be streamed directly to the processor.
Meanwhile the normal ear does not hear; the person listens only through the implant and tries to understand speech.
Short listening sessions done every day help develop speech understanding with the implanted ear.
In programming, implant loudness is balanced with the normal ear; sound should feel balanced, not piled up on one side.
The implant will sound different from the normal ear; it is explained from the start that this is expected.

sahneler.metin: Explain all options to a person with single-sided deafness without bias. A trial of CROS or a bone-conduction device on a band before surgery clarifies expectations.
cumleler: A tip from the clinic: at the first visit, explain all options to a person with single-sided deafness fairly, with pros and limits.
Before the surgical decision, trying CROS or a bone-conduction device on a band in everyday settings clarifies the person's needs.
Because duration of deafness affects implant outcome, refer a person interested in an implant for evaluation without delay.
For a person who develops single-sided deafness after sudden hearing loss, plan this visit after medical treatment is complete.

maddeler.metin: CROS and bone conduction: reroute sound

cumleler: Single-sided deafness impairs localization and hearing in noise, raises listening effort and often comes with tinnitus.
CROS and bone-conduction devices carry sound from the deaf side to the good ear; but they do not restore two-eared hearing.
A cochlear implant stimulates the deaf ear itself; benefits are reported for localization, some noise conditions and tinnitus.
Outcome depends on duration of deafness, the state of the cochlear nerve and regular use; criteria vary by country.

sahneler.soru: Which option aims to restore localization?
sahneler.aciklama: The implant stimulates _the deaf ear itself_; the others carry sound to the good ear.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: in single-sided deafness, which option aims to restore localization?

cumleler: The correct answer is C: a cochlear implant.
CROS and bone-conduction devices carry sound to one cochlea; the implant gives the deaf ear its own input, aiming for two-eared hearing.
